passages.t: Look to the rock you were cut from
passages.happening:
God speaks to those ‘who pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD’ (verse 1). ‘Look to the rock from which you were cut, and to the quarry from which you were hewn’ (verse 1). ‘Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who gave you birth’ (verse 2). When God called Abraham he was only one, and God made him many.

‘For the LORD will comfort Zion and will look with compassion on all her ruins’ (verse 3). He will make her wilderness like Eden and her desert like the garden of the LORD. Joy, thanksgiving and song will be found there.

A law will go out from God, and his justice will become a light to the nations (verse 4). His salvation is on the way, and the islands wait for his arm (verse 5). The heavens will vanish like smoke and the earth wear out like a garment, ‘But My salvation will last forever, and My righteousness will never fail’ (verse 6).

Those who have God's law in their hearts are not to fear people's scorn (verse 7). ‘For the moth will devour them like a garment’ (verse 8), but God's righteousness lasts through all generations.
passages.hearers:
Chapter 50 ended with a call to trust the LORD in the dark. Chapter 51 speaks to those very people, who seek the LORD but see only ruins.

The look back to Abraham mattered to a community that had lost its land, its king and its temple. Ezekiel records people in ruined Judah using the same memory to argue that, since Abraham was one man and they were many, the land must be theirs. Isaiah uses it the other way. Not that they deserve the land, but that God can make much out of little. One old man and one barren woman became a nation.

The word comfort appears four times in the chapter, taking up the opening words of chapter 40. The comfort is not a feeling offered from far away. It is God's own presence and action, turning ruins into a garden.

Three times God calls the people to listen to him (verses 1, 4 and 7). Each call carries a promise.
passages.later: Ezekiel heard the people in the ruins argue, ‘Abraham was only one man, yet he possessed the land’ (Ezekiel 33:24). Hebrews tells the same story of Abraham: ‘from one man, and he as good as dead, came descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky’ (Hebrews 11:12).
passages.asks: God tells a discouraged people to look back to where they came from. Ask what in your own story shows God making much out of little. And ask whose scorn you fear, and what it would mean that it will wear out like a garment.

passages.t: Awake, arm of the LORD, and God's reply
passages.happening:
The people cry out. ‘Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD’ (verse 9). Wake as in days past. ‘Was it not You who cut Rahab to pieces, who pierced through the dragon?’ (verse 9). ‘Was it not You who dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep, who made a road in the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross over?’ (verse 10).

‘So the redeemed of the LORD will return and enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy’ (verse 11). Sorrow and sighing will flee.

God answers. ‘I, even I, am He who comforts you’ (verse 12). Why are they afraid of mortal men who wither like grass? They have forgotten the LORD their Maker, who stretched out the heavens, and they live in terror of the oppressor all day long. ‘But where is the fury of the oppressor?’ (verse 13). ‘The captive will soon be freed; he will not die in the dungeon’ (verse 14). God has put his words in their mouth and covered them with the shadow of his hand (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The chapter speaks to a people who feel small and exposed. Many had seen family members deported, imprisoned or killed. The promise that the captive will not die in the dungeon spoke to that fear directly.

Verses 9 and 10 use pictures known across the ancient world, where the raging sea often stood for chaos. Clay tablets from Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, found from 1929 onward, tell of the storm god Baal defeating Yam, the Sea, and a coiling sea monster. The Old Testament borrows the language without the mythology. Rahab here is not the woman of Jericho. It is a name for a sea monster, and elsewhere a poetic name for Egypt. The prophet joins creation and exodus: the God who mastered the chaos waters is the God who dried up the sea to make a road for the redeemed.

The people ask God to wake up. God's reply shows that he is not the one asleep. They have forgotten him.
passages.later: A psalm uses the same picture: ‘You crushed Rahab like a carcass; You scattered Your enemies with Your mighty arm’ (Psalm 89:10). Verse 11 repeats almost word for word the promise of Isaiah 35:10, that the redeemed will return to Zion with singing.
passages.hard:
Does Isaiah believe the old stories of a god fighting a sea monster?

The prophet uses language his hearers knew from the wider world, as poets do, but he empties it of its mythology. In the Ugarit stories the sea is a rival god. In Isaiah there is no rival. The sea and the dragon are creatures, and the LORD has mastered them. Rahab is also used in Scripture as a nickname for Egypt (Isaiah 30:7; Psalm 87:4), so the picture slides at once into the crossing of the sea at the exodus.

Readers differ on how much of the older imagery Israel's poets had in mind. All agree that the passage uses it to say the opposite of what the myths said: there is one God, and the chaos is under his hand.
passages.asks: The people call on God to wake up, and God tells them they have forgotten him. Ask whether you have ever prayed as if God were asleep. And ask what oppressor you live in fear of, and where its fury will be in the end.

passages.t: Jerusalem, wake up: the cup taken away
passages.happening:
Now God turns the cry around. “Awake, awake! Rise up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of His fury” (verse 17). She has drained the goblet to the dregs, the cup that makes people stagger.

Among all the sons she raised, no one is there to guide her or take her hand (verse 18). ‘These pairs have befallen you: devastation and destruction, famine and sword’ (verse 19). ‘Who will grieve for you? Who can comfort you?’ (verse 19). Her sons lie faint at the head of every street, like an antelope in a net (verse 20).

So she is to hear this, ‘you afflicted one, drunken, but not with wine’ (verse 21). God, who defends his people, says he has taken the cup of staggering from her hand, and she will never drink it again (verse 22). He will put it into the hands of her tormentors, who made her lie down so they could walk over her back like a street (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The images fit the time after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC: young men lying faint in the streets, devastation, famine and sword.

The cup of wrath was a well known picture in the prophets. Jeremiah was told to make the nations drink the cup of God's wrath until they staggered, and a psalm pictures the LORD holding a foaming cup that the wicked must drain. It is drunkenness without wine, a people reeling and helpless under judgment.

Verse 23 draws on the custom of conquerors humiliating the defeated by treading on them. Joshua's commanders put their feet on the necks of captured kings. Here the oppressors who walked on Jerusalem's back will drink the cup themselves.

This is the second of the double calls to wake. The people asked God to wake (verse 9). God replies that it is Jerusalem who must wake, because the cup is gone.
passages.later: Jeremiah was told, “Take from My hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink from it” (Jeremiah 25:15), and a psalm says the wicked drink God's cup ‘down to the dregs’ (Psalm 75:8).
passages.hard:
Jerusalem is said to have drunk the cup of God's fury, and her sons lie faint in the streets. How should a reader carry that?

The passage is spoken to Judah about Judah's own catastrophe, and its point is that the cup has been taken away. It is not a key for reading anyone else's suffering. It gives no warrant to blame the Jewish people, and no warrant to call any people's suffering, then or now, a punishment they deserved. The prophet asks who will grieve for Jerusalem, and God himself answers as the one who comforts.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God takes the cup from Jerusalem's hand and says she will never drink it again. Ask what it would mean to believe that a judgment in your life has ended. And ask who around you has no one to take their hand, as Jerusalem had no one.
